source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5209286 (accepted author manuscript): abstract, graphical-abstract legend, all sections (Dopamine; HVA; DAT; VMAT2; nigral cellularity; gliosis; clinical parkinsonism; Comment; Conclusions), the Table (HTML) and acknowledgments read in full; reference list checked for the cited imaging, post-mortem and epidemiological studies.

claims.note: Supports 'lower on average' qualitatively (no effect sizes): striatal DAT reduction called the most replicated dopamine-marker finding in methamphetamine users (post-mortem binding and Western blot, post-mortem immunohistochemistry, and imaging). Supports the claim's interpretive sentence in part: the cause is 'still argued' (compensatory down-regulation, loss of transporter protein, or loss of neurone), and DAT can normalize with abstinence. It does not mention pre-existing differences. The imaging list includes Schouw et al. 2013, a study of recreational dexamphetamine users, and the text says 'seven independent' studies while citing ten papers (several from the same groups).

anchors.locator: Dopamine Transporter > Methamphetamine users: Striatal dopamine transporter is reduced: Why?, paras 1-2
anchors.extracted: Lower striatal DAT post-mortem (Wilson 1996a; Kitamura 2007) and in 'seven independent' PET/SPECT studies (ten papers cited: McCann 1998, 2008; Sekine 2001, 2003; Volkow 2001a, 2001b; Johanson 2006; Chou 2007; Schouw 2013; Yuan 2014). Cause still argued: compensation for low dopamine, loss of transporter protein, or loss of part or all of the neurone; Volkow 2001a (and Chou 2007, Volkow 2015) suggest normalization with extended abstinence.

claims.note: This source supplies the claim's last sentence: post-mortem VMAT2 binding normal (Wilson 1996a, at a saturating ligand concentration; Kitamura 2007 n.s. with a trend to reduction in accumbens and putamen) and about 10% lower PET binding in users 'reputedly' abstinent about three years (Johanson 2006). It also restates the Boileau results (raised in under a week of abstinence, normal at 7-15 days) and the competition interpretation. Cross-source discrepancy for the editors: Ashok et al. (2017) describe the Johanson 2006 users as abstinent about three months, Kish 2017 as about three years; the primary paper should be checked before writing 'long-abstinent'. Kish 2017 is co-authored by Boileau, so it is not independent of Boileau 2016's interpretation.

anchors.locator: Vesicular Monoamine Transporter (VMAT2) > Methamphetamine users: ... normal/near-normal or elevated, paras 1-4
anchors.extracted: Two post-mortem studies (Wilson 1996a normal; Kitamura 2007 no significant difference) and three PET studies: Johanson 2006 binding about 10% lower in users reputedly abstinent for three years; Boileau 2008 and 2016a higher binding in early abstinence (under a week) and normal at 7-15 days. Authors attribute the early rise to less competition from depleted vesicular dopamine (citing dopa-responsive dystonia as an analogue); overall 'no or at most a slight loss' of VMAT2.

claims.note: Every element of the claim is in this source: 'premature' to conclude either way; marker changes cannot distinguish terminal loss from regulation (the authors' 'biochemical marker confound'); DAT normalizes with abstinence and VMAT2 binding is normal after 1-2 weeks; the pattern differs from Parkinson's disease (only dopamine and DAT low, metabolites, synthetic enzymes and VMAT2 normal; caudate more affected than putamen, the reverse of PD); and no quantitative counts of nigral cells or striatal terminals exist in human users (magnitude field). It also qualifies: animal data predict damage at some, probably high, dose; two registry studies are 'consistent with' damage in a subgroup; two individuals had near-total (95%, 97%) caudate dopamine loss; and the post-mortem dopamine data come from one laboratory and are unreplicated. Authors' own work dominates the evidence reviewed.

anchors.extracted: Authors judge it premature to conclude whether recreational doses cause or do not cause loss of, or damage to, dopamine neurones in humans.

anchors.locator: Table; Comment > But does methamphetamine cause loss of all or part of dopamine neurones?
anchors.extracted: Post-mortem striatum: in PD all markers decreased (dopamine, HVA/DOPAC/3-MT, TH/AADC, VMAT2, DAT, nigral cellularity); in methamphetamine users only dopamine and DAT decreased, metabolites and enzymes normal, VMAT2 normal to slightly decreased, nigral cellularity unknown (no 'obvious' loss).

anchors.locator: Methamphetamine users: One (Toronto) laboratory reports low brain dopamine, paras 2-4
anchors.extracted: 20 users (all drug-positive at autopsy, last use within about 5 days) vs 14 controls and 12 PD cases: dopamine -61% caudate, -50% putamen in users; PD -82% caudate, -97% putamen; finding from one laboratory, unreplicated, called preliminary; low dopamine could reflect depletion in intact neurones and/or neurone loss.

anchors.locator: Substantia Nigra Cellularity > Methamphetamine users; Conclusions, paras 3-4
anchors.extracted: No quantitative nigral cell counts in users (qualitative: no obvious loss); no post-mortem studies of structural striatal terminal damage in users; markers can be up- or down-regulated independently of neuropil, so marker loss cannot be equated with terminal loss.

DAT normalizes with extended abstinence (Volkow 2001a; Chou 2007; Volkow 2015); VMAT2 binding normal by 7-15 days; authors speculate low dopamine is acute, partly reversible depletion and low DAT a reversible compensatory down-regulation (explicitly labelled speculation).

anchors.locator: Introduction and Objective, para 2; Does Methamphetamine Cause Clinical Parkinsonism?; Comment para 1; Brain Gliosis section
anchors.extracted: Animal findings predict damage at some unknown, probably high, dose; registry HRs (California 1.76, Utah 2.8) 'consistent with' damage in a subgroup; two users had 95% and 97% caudate dopamine loss ('Parkinsonian range'); gliosis status uncertain (one PET study reported 250-1500% higher PK11195 binding, methodologically uncertain).

claims.note: Source of the California figure: HR 1.76 (95% CI 1.12-2.75) vs an appendicitis proxy-control group, follow-up up to 16 years in statewide inpatient data, with no increase in a cocaine group; also restates Utah HR 2.8 (1.6-4.8). The authors add that the associations are not proof and imply only a very small proportion of users are later diagnosed with PD. Two of the four Kish 2017 authors (Kish, Callaghan) authored the California studies (Callaghan et al. 2010 and 2012a are both cited for the HR), so this is self-report, not independent confirmation; the primary paper should be read before final grading, as the claim already notes.

anchors.locator: Does Methamphetamine Cause Clinical Parkinsonism in the Human?, para 2
anchors.extracted: California inpatient cohort, methamphetamine/amphetamine-related conditions followed up to 16 years: HR 1.76 (95% CI 1.12-2.75) for PD vs appendicitis group; cocaine group not increased (Callaghan et al. 2010, 2012a). Utah: HR 2.8 (1.6-4.8) (Curtin 2015). Associations not proof; only a very small proportion of users later diagnosed.

key_findings.correction: The text says 'seven independent PET/SPECT imaging studies' while citing ten papers; read as seven groups (McCann x2, Sekine x2, Volkow x2, Johanson, Chou, Schouw, Yuan) the card's 'seven independent groups' is a fair interpretation.

The 'biochemical marker confound' argument and the statement that structural terminal damage has not been examined post-mortem in users are in Conclusions, 3rd paragraph ('Assuming for the sake of argument that nigral dopamine cellularity is spared...'); the 2nd paragraph holds the labelled speculations (reversible depletion; compensatory DAT down-regulation).

reporting_issues.note: Checked against the task files: project volkow_2001a = Am J Psychiatry 158:377 (psychomotor), volkow_2001b = J Neurosci 21:9414 (recovery); Kish 2017 text uses 2001a for the recovery follow-up.
Found independently in step 1 (Ashok: 'after three months of abstinence'; Kish 2017: 'reputedly withdrawn for three years').

risk_of_bias.note: The domain judgments are reasonable, but the instrument choice is inconsistent with the other narrative-review cards in this batch (Bramness 2012, Glasner-Edwards 2014 and Kish 2008 were rated with AMSTAR 2, critically low, 'for consistency'). Either apply AMSTAR 2 here too (it would also be critically low) or record 'none-applicable' on all four; the editors should pick one rule.

missed: Comment > Marked dopamine loss..., para 2: two users in the authors' post-mortem series had near-total caudate dopamine loss (95% and 97%, in the 'Parkinsonian range'), which the authors think likely caused some behavioural impairment. This qualifies the 'not established' framing of cl_meth_dopamine_damage (severe depletion exists in some individuals even if neurone loss is unproven) and is not on the card.

The California HR (1.76, 1.12-2.75) is cited to both Callaghan et al. 2010 (Mov Disord) and 2012a (Drug Alcohol Depend), both co-authored by Kish; the card's funding note records the overlap, but cl_meth_parkinson currently rests the California figure on this review alone.

Introduction para 1 reports an all-cause standardized mortality ratio of 4.67 in the authors' California methamphetamine cohort (Callaghan et al. 2012b); not needed for the assigned claims, noted for completeness.
